(from miš ḥayḥṣal abadan) · d) ʾalbi ʾayilli Innu gay. · e) lāzim tḥawwiš ḥāga kull šahr. · f) ili fāt māt. Exercise 7. Personal answer. The tutor checks that the line is correctly transcribed and that the explanation identifies what it plays (word, situation, character). Exercise 8. a) That he's funny, funny; the opposite is dammu tʾīl, unpleasant, heavy. The joke (hazār) is normal among friends; the teasing (tarʾīʾa) has a bad intention. Better timing and a good closure. Because Luke's phrase (I must also learn the joke with effect) was itself a witty and well placed. b) A couch, a table and a rug, and he's out of money. •Stretch your legs according to the blanket (live according to your means); White money serves on the black day (save for difficult times); What has passed is dead (do not think about it). Water passed no more millstones. Because Luke speaks for proverbs like old ladies. c) Who drives as in a race and who, like the comedian, drives as on a tour. On an exaggeration: for a ten-minute journey it took an hour and a half, as if living at Aswān, very far away. If he's late, it's a problem. If the boss arrives soon, he thinks he's sick. Span the legs according to the blanket, and according to traffic... stay at home! 1. the Dammaha bint ḫafīf ʾawi. · 2. ir-rāgil dammu tʾīl. · 3.
